name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: A Unified Gateway and SDK for Calling 100+ LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python SDK from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and model providers, so a reader deciding whether to use it should know that the project is mid-migration from a Python proxy to a Rust core, and that the Rust gateway is still an early beta.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and lives at github.com/BerriAI/litellm, with documentation at docs.litellm.ai. It is a gateway and client library rather than a model or a training framework. The site describes it as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, a Rust core with a Python SDK, and the repository lists Python as its language with a custom licence. It sits in the serving and routing layer of the AI stack, between application code and model providers, translating requests to more than 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format. The repository shows a last push on 3 October 2026 and roughly 60,083 stars. The site does not state a first release date, so when it first appeared is not settled by the material read.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are routing and governing model traffic: calling many providers through one interface, tracking spend, applying budgets and rate limits, load balancing across model groups, caching responses in Redis, logging requests, and enforcing guardrails. The site also documents an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway, so agents, model calls and tool access can share one control plane, with per-user and per-team attribution through headers such as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id. Reliability testing is covered too, with batch_completion_models_all_responses sending one conversation to every model in parallel and returning only the responses that succeeded. It is strongest where a team needs one policy and billing surface across many providers, and where gateway overhead matters, which is the case the Rust work is built around.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone who has called an LLM API, since the surface is largely OpenAI-shaped, and the site's tutorials are code examples rather than theory. The gateway side asks more of you: production deployments involve Redis, keys, teams, budgets, rate limits, model groups, SSO or SAML, audit logs and Kubernetes, so some systems and operations knowledge helps. The site does not present a structured beginner course, and it does not state formal mathematics prerequisites, which is reasonable for a routing layer rather than a training library. A beginner can start from the tutorials, but should expect the operational material to be the harder half.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site names integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and the tutorials reference models such as gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-terra, claude-sonnet-5 and a replicate/llama-2-70b-chat model. It documents an A2A JSON-RPC interface for invoking shared agents, MCP servers with OAuth2 authorization code flow and PKCE, OIDC authentication, and a LiteAdmin MCP connector that lets an agent work through the gateway's management API, with a Slack admin agent built on it. Documentation is extensive, with 60 pages read, including tutorials, blog posts, incident reports and release notes. The repository's star count suggests a large audience, though the site does not publish contributor or forum numbers, so community size beyond that is not established here.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: It is aimed at both, with different costs. The Python SDK and proxy make quick experiments easy, and the tutorials show short scripts for testing providers and load. The production story is where the site is most detailed, and also where the trade-offs show. The Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and the site says pods get OOM-killed at the worst time. The Rust gateway is reported to serve about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms, and deploying as a single binary. That Rust gateway is an early beta, so the performance figures are the project's own benchmark rather than a settled production guarantee.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site describes production use with SSO or SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails, and incident reports reference an enterprise customer running litellm-database behind nginx, so adoption includes real enterprise deployments. It is a current choice rather than a legacy one, with active releases, a Rust migration under way and a stated commitment to a pure Rust server serving all AI traffic. For someone choosing what to learn, the gateway and routing skills transfer across providers, and the Python SDK is a low-cost entry. The site does not name customers or publish adoption statistics, so how widely it is used across the industry is not something the material settles.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, and the site positions it against other gateways, benchmarking the Rust gateway against Portkey, Bifrost and the current LiteLLM Python proxy. It is typically used with provider SDKs and APIs rather than replacing them, calling Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx instead of importing the mistralai package, and it works alongside Redis for caching and rate limiting, Kubernetes for deployment, and identity providers through OIDC, SSO or SAML. The polyglot pattern is a Python application or agent talking to a gateway that speaks many provider protocols, with MCP for tools and A2A for agent-to-agent calls. The site does not document bindings for other languages, so use outside Python and Rust is not established.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about failures. A Medium severity incident in v1.100.0 caused kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS, and thousands of 502s and 499s, triggered by unbounded retry breadcrumb growth when Redis was unreachable, fixed in v1.100.1. Another Medium incident in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1 silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend 2-3x, fixed in v1.91.2. The site also notes that server-side Claude Code auto mode depends on a contract some gateways did not preserve, LiteLLM included, with a fix merged and shipping through dev, release candidate and stable releases. The Rust gateway is an early beta, and the benchmark comparing it with Portkey and Bifrost is the project's own. The site does not state a stable release date for the Rust server, does not publish independent performance reviews, and does not say how the custom licence affects commercial use, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
